title: Still Face Raw Import (Python)
text:
This is a Python port of Still Face Raw Import, built to run side by side with the R version as a demonstration of moving the same real analysis pipeline between R and Python.
It reads the same raw per-subject event log exports (one Excel file per subject) and turns them into ONE wide dataset – one row per subject, one column per scored variable – following the exact same rules as the R version:

Read every subject’s raw Excel event log.
Check each file for basic problems (wrong ID, unrecognized behavioral codes).
Find the Baseline / Still Face / Reunion episode boundaries for that subject (the “anchors”).
Label every row with which episode it falls in.
Compute every duration/count/joint-attention variable, per episode.
Reshape each subject from long (one row per coded event) to wide (one row per subject).
Stack every subject into one dataset and check for duplicate IDs.

What this file does NOT do: it does not save anything. In the source project the R version writes the merged dataset to SPSS for 6M_Still_Face_Compute.sps to pick up; this portfolio page only demonstrates the pipeline and previews an aggregate summary of the result, consistent with the rest of this site.


This page runs Python through R’s reticulate package (via engine: knitr above) rather than a Jupyter kernel, so the only extra runtime dependency is a local Python 3 install with pandas, numpy, and openpyxl.


Show code
import re
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd





Same as the R version – PROJECT_ROOT is the only line a new user should need to change. Every other path is built from it.

section: Import one subject’s file and run basic checks
text:
Import one subject’s file and run basic checks


Show code
# Running log of blank/empty template rows found and dropped, across every
# subject processed. Mirrors the R version's BLANK_ROW_LOG.
BLANK_ROW_LOG: list[dict] = []


def import_event_log(filename_full: Path) -> pd.DataFrame:
    filename_short = filename_full.name
    filename_id = extract_id_from_filename(filename_short)

    data = pd.read_excel(filename_full)

    # Identify blank template rows: no Behavior coded at all, and both the
    # relative time and duration are exactly 0 -- these are empty leftover
    # rows in the export, not real coded data.
    blank_rows = data[
        data["Behavior"].isna() & (data["Time_Relative_sf"] == 0) & (data["Duration_sf"] == 0)
    ]
    if len(blank_rows) > 0:
        BLANK_ROW_LOG.append(
            {"ID": filename_id, "file": filename_short, "n_blank_rows": len(blank_rows)}
        )
        data = data[
            ~(data["Behavior"].isna() & (data["Time_Relative_sf"] == 0) & (data["Duration_sf"] == 0))
        ]

    # Time_Relative_hms comes in as an Excel time-of-day value. openpyxl
    # hands these back as either a bare duration (timedelta64) or a full
    # datetime with a fake date attached, depending on the cell's exact
    # number format, so both need to be handled to land on plain
    # "HH:MM:SS" text.
    data = data.copy()
    hms_col = data["Time_Relative_hms"]
    if pd.api.types.is_timedelta64_dtype(hms_col):
        total_seconds = hms_col.dt.total_seconds().astype(int)
    else:
        total_seconds = (
            pd.to_datetime(hms_col).dt.hour * 3600
            + pd.to_datetime(hms_col).dt.minute * 60
            + pd.to_datetime(hms_col).dt.second
        )
    data["Time_Relative_hms"] = [
        f"{s // 3600:02d}:{(s % 3600) // 60:02d}:{s % 60:02d}" for s in total_seconds
    ]

    # Number every row in a new column called "Code". This is the
    # event-order counter the rest of the script uses to find episode
    # boundaries.
    data = data.reset_index(drop=True)
    data.insert(0, "Code", data.index + 1)
    data["ID"] = data["Subject ID"].astype(str)

    # Stop if the file contains more than one Subject ID.
    internal_ids = data["ID"].unique()
    if len(internal_ids) != 1:
        raise ValueError(
            f"File does not contain exactly one Subject ID: {filename_short}. "
            f"Found: {', '.join(internal_ids)}"
        )

    # Stop if the ID inside the file doesn't match the ID in the file name.
    if internal_ids[0] != filename_id:
        raise ValueError(
            f"File name ID ({filename_id}) does not match internal Subject ID "
            f"({internal_ids[0]}) in file: {filename_short}"
        )

    # Pull out every Subject/Behavior combination in this file that ISN'T an
    # episode marker, and compare against BEHAVIOR_REFERENCE.
    observed = data.loc[~data["Behavior"].isin(EPISODE_MARKERS), ["Subject", "Behavior"]].drop_duplicates()
    unmapped = observed.merge(
        BEHAVIOR_REFERENCE[["Subject", "Behavior"]], on=["Subject", "Behavior"], how="left", indicator=True
    ).query('_merge == "left_only"')

    if len(unmapped) > 0:
        pairs = "; ".join(f"{s}/{b}" for s, b in zip(unmapped["Subject"], unmapped["Behavior"]))
        raise ValueError(
            f"Unrecognized Subject/Behavior combination(s) in file {filename_short}: {pairs}. "
            "Add to BEHAVIOR_REFERENCE or fix the coding before re-running."
        )

    return data

title: Still Face Raw Import
text:
This R syntax file takes the raw per-subject event log exports @still-face-data-example (one Excel file per subject) and turns them into ONE wide dataset – one row per subject, one column per scored variable – ready to be further scored in SPSS.
Step by step, it:

Reads every subject’s raw Excel event log.
Checks each file for basic problems (wrong ID, unrecognized behavioral codes).
Finds the Baseline / Still Face / Reunion episode boundaries for that subject (the “anchors”).
Labels every row with which episode it falls in.
Computes every duration/count/joint-attention variable, per episode.
Reshapes each subject from long (one row per coded event) to wide (one row per subject).
Stacks every subject into one dataset and checks for duplicate IDs.
In the source project, saves that one merged, wide dataset as an SPSS .sav file.

Load required packages


Show code
# Core data-wrangling verbs (filter, mutate, pivot_wider, the pipe, etc)
library(tidyverse)
# Reads .xlsx files -- needed for the raw event log export
library(readxl)

title: Still Face Raw Import
text:
Behavior reference table
BEHAVIOR_REFERENCE lists every Subject/Behavior combination we expect to see in a raw file. Built into the pipeline is a data validation check - the import process stops if a file contains a Subject/Behavior code that isn’t in this table – most likely cause would be a typo in the coding software, or an addition of a code after the scoring pipeline was created.
category groups related behaviors together for readability and organization. var_stem is the short suffix that ends up in the final prefixed variable names (see the @score-spec section below).


Show code
BEHAVIOR_REFERENCE <- tribble(
  ~Subject,  ~Behavior,                          ~category,               ~var_stem,

  # --- infant gaze: who the infant is looking at ---
  # infant looking at mom
  "Infant",  "Looking at Mom",                   "infant_gaze",        "yeslook",
  # infant looking away from mom
  "Infant",  "Looking Away",                     "infant_gaze",        "notlook",
  # infant's gaze could not be coded (face/eyes not visible on video)
  "Infant",  "Infant Gaze Not Visible",           "infant_gaze",        "gaze_nv",

  # --- infant facial expression ---
  # neutral facial expression
  "Infant",  "Neutral Expression",               "infant_expression",  "neuexp",
  # smiling / positive facial expression
  "Infant",  "Smile/Positive Expression",        "infant_expression",  "posexp",
  # frowning / negative facial expression
  "Infant",  "Frown/Negative Expression",        "infant_expression",  "negexp",
  # infant's face could not be coded (not visible on video)
  "Infant",  "Infant Face Not Visible",           "infant_expression",  "face_nv",

  # --- infant vocalization ---
  # infant not vocalizing
  "Infant",  "Infant Silent",                    "infant_vocal",       "silvoc",
  # neutral vocalization
  "Infant",  "Neutral Vocal",                    "infant_vocal",       "neuvoc",
  # laughing / positive vocalization
  "Infant",  "Laughing/Positive Vocal",          "infant_vocal",       "posvoc",
  # crying / negative vocalization
  "Infant",  "Crying/Negative Vocal",            "infant_vocal",       "negvoc",

  # --- infant orientation (Still Face episode only) ---
  # infant oriented toward an object rather than the parent
  "Infant",  "Object Orientation",               "infant_orientation", "obj",
  # infant oriented toward the parent
  "Infant",  "Parent Orientation",               "infant_orientation", "par",

  # --- infant discrete self-soothing/escape actions (Still Face only) ---
  # infant engaging in a self-comforting behavior
  "Infant",  "Infant Comforting",                "infant_action",      "comf",
  # infant engaging in an escape behavior (e.g., arching away)
  "Infant",  "Infant Escape",                    "infant_action",      "esc",

  # --- mother/parent affect ---
  # high-intensity negative affect
  "Mother",  "High Negative Affect",             "mother_affect",      "negaffH",
  # low-intensity negative affect
  "Mother",  "Negative Affect",                  "mother_affect",      "negaffL",
  # neutral affect
  "Mother",  "Neutral Affect",                   "mother_affect",      "neuaff",
  # low-intensity positive affect
  "Mother",  "Positive Affect",                  "mother_affect",      "posaffL",
  # high-intensity positive affect
  "Mother",  "High Positive Affect",             "mother_affect",      "posaffH",
  # affect not visible
  "Mother", "Mom Affect Not Visible",            "mother_affect",      "noaffect", #ID107

  # --- mother talking/touching the infant ---
  # mom is talking to and/or touching the infant
  "Mother",  "Mom Talking/Touching Infant",      "mother_talktouch",   "tlktch",
  # mom is NOT talking to or touching the infant
  "Mother",  "Mom NOT Talking/Touching Infant",  "mother_talktouch",   "nottlktch"
)

title: Baseline Warmth Data Import, Processing, and Reliability
text:
This file performs two related tasks for baseline observational warmth coding.
First, it imports the original baseline CARMA files, processes each video beginning at second 6, creates the four Mom/Partner × Negative/Positive warmth datasets in R, merges them by couple ID, and saves one final SPSS dataset (BL_WH.sav). The workflow includes data-quality stop points so that invalid warmth values, duplicate IDs, duplicate seconds, or unexpected CARMA timing cannot silently enter the final dataset.
Second, sections 5–9 below import the separate reliability-coded CARMA files, process them using the same second-by-second cleaning rules, match them to the corresponding original-coded observations, and calculate inter-rater reliability. Reliability data stay in R and are not added to BL_WH.sav.
Warmth values of 0 are converted to NA during processing so that SPSS reads them as system-missing values and they are excluded from average warmth scores.

title: Baseline Warmth Data Import, Processing, and Reliability
text:
Update the Box file path

title: Baseline Warmth Data Import, Processing, and Reliability
text:
Load required R packages
These packages are used to import files, reshape the second-by-second warmth data, combine datasets, and (in the source project) export the final SPSS .sav file. tidyverse is used for file processing, reshaping, and matching. haven creates the SPSS dataset. irr is used for the ICC reliability calculation.


Show code
library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(irr)

title: Baseline Warmth Data Import, Processing, and Reliability
section: Extract the couple ID from a file name
text:
Extract the couple ID from a file name
Original CARMA files are stored in couple folders such as Couple 101/101BL_M_NEG_WH_GG.csv. Reliability files also begin with the couple number, such as 124BL_M_POS_WH_RC.csv.
The function below extracts the three-digit couple ID from the beginning of the CSV file name.
The script stops if a file does not begin with a three-digit ID rather than assigning an incorrect ID.


Show code
extract_couple_id <- function(filename) {

  # Extract the first three digits from the base file name.
  id <- str_extract(basename(filename), "^\\d{3}")

  # Stop if a three-digit ID cannot be identified.
  if (is.na(id)) {
    stop("Could not identify a three-digit couple ID from file: ", basename(filename))
  }

  id
}

title: Baseline Warmth Data Import, Processing, and Reliability
text:
Process one CARMA warmth file
This function contains the core cleaning rules that should be identical for every CARMA file. It imports one CSV and returns a standardized long dataset containing one row per coded second.
For each file, the function:

Imports the first two CARMA columns as second and warmth.
Converts the second column to numeric and explicitly locates second 6.
Stops if second 6 is missing or appears more than once.
Keeps the coding window beginning exactly at second 6, regardless of how many metadata rows precede it.
Stops if duplicate seconds occur within the retained coding window.
Extracts the couple ID from the beginning of the file name.
Converts warmth to numeric and stops if an observed value is outside the valid 0–7 range.
Truncates valid warmth values to whole-number codes to match the existing processing convention.
Converts warmth 0 to NA.

Keeping these rules in one function ensures that CARMA files are processed in exactly the same way.


Show code
process_single_warmth_file <- function(filename_full) {

  # Keep the base file name for readable error messages and documentation.
  filename_short <- basename(filename_full)

  # Import the full CARMA export without assuming a fixed number of metadata rows.
  data <- read.csv(filename_full) %>%
    as.data.frame()

  # Stop if the CARMA export does not contain at least two columns.
  if (ncol(data) < 2) {
    stop("Expected at least two columns in file: ", filename_short)
  }

  # Retain and standardize the two CARMA columns used in processing.
  data <- data[, 1:2]
  names(data) <- c("second", "warmth")

  # Convert the second column to numeric so the start of the coding window can be located.
  data <- data %>%
    mutate(second = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(second))))

  # Locate the single row corresponding to second 6.
  second_6_rows <- which(!is.na(data$second) & data$second == 6)

  # Stop if the start of the required coding window cannot be identified uniquely.
  if (length(second_6_rows) == 0) {
    stop("Could not find second 6 in file: ", filename_short)
  }

  if (length(second_6_rows) > 1) {
    stop("Second 6 appears more than once in file: ", filename_short)
  }

  # Keep only the intended coding window from second 6 through second 600.
  # If a CARMA file extended beyond 600 seconds, later seconds are excluded.
  data <- data[second_6_rows:nrow(data), , drop = FALSE] %>%
    filter(second <= 600)

  # Remove rows after the coded time series that do not contain a numeric second.
  data <- data %>%
    filter(!is.na(second))

  # Stop if seconds are duplicated within the retained coding window.
  duplicate_seconds <- unique(data$second[duplicated(data$second)])

  if (length(duplicate_seconds) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Duplicate second values found after second 6 in file ",
      filename_short, ": ", paste(duplicate_seconds, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  # Confirm that the retained coding window begins at second 6.
  if (nrow(data) == 0 || data$second[1] != 6) {
    stop("Retained coding window does not begin at second 6 in file: ", filename_short)
  }

  # Extract the three-digit couple ID from the beginning of the file name.
  couple_id <- extract_couple_id(filename_short)

  # Convert warmth values to numeric using the same order as the original working syntax.
  data <- data %>%
    mutate(warmth = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(warmth))))

  # Remove decimals before validation, matching manual of whole number codes.
  data <- data %>%
    mutate(warmth = trunc(warmth))

  # Stop if any processed nonmissing warmth value falls outside the valid 0-7 coding range.
  invalid_warmth <- data %>%
    filter(!is.na(warmth), warmth < 0 | warmth > 7)

  if (nrow(invalid_warmth) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Processed warmth value outside the valid 0-7 range for ID ",
      couple_id, " in file: ", filename_short,
      ". Offending second(s): ",
      paste(invalid_warmth$second, collapse = ", "),
      ". Value(s): ",
      paste(invalid_warmth$warmth, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  # Convert code 0 to R missing so SPSS imports it as system missing.
  data <- data %>%
    mutate(warmth = na_if(warmth, 0))

  # Return one standardized row per coded second.
  data %>%
    transmute(
      ID = couple_id,
      second = second,
      warmth = warmth,
      source_file = filename_short
    )
}

title: Baseline Warmth Data Import, Processing, and Reliability
section: Process one original baseline warmth condition
text:
Process one original baseline warmth condition
This wrapper finds all original CARMA files matching one condition (BL_M_NEG, BL_P_NEG, BL_M_POS, or BL_P_POS), sends every file through the single-file processing function, and then converts the standardized long data into the wide format used in the final SPSS dataset.
Before processing, the function checks that only one source file exists for each couple within that condition. Duplicate IDs in the finished wide dataset are checked later by the dataset validation function.


Show code
process_warmth_files <- function(path, pattern, variable_prefix, average_name) {

  # Find all CSV files matching the requested original warmth condition.
  files_full <- list.files(
    path = path,
    pattern = paste0(pattern, ".*\\.csv$"),
    full.names = TRUE,
    recursive = TRUE,
    ignore.case = TRUE
  )

  # Stop if no matching files are found.
  if (length(files_full) == 0) {
    stop("No files found for pattern: ", pattern)
  }

  # Extract the couple ID from each matching base file name.
  file_ids <- map_chr(files_full, extract_couple_id)

  # Stop before processing if more than one source file maps to the same couple ID.
  duplicate_source_ids <- unique(file_ids[duplicated(file_ids)])

  if (length(duplicate_source_ids) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Duplicate source files found for ", pattern, " IDs: ",
      paste(duplicate_source_ids, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  # Process every source file with the common second-by-second cleaning function.
  dataset_long <- map_dfr(files_full, process_single_warmth_file)

  # Reshape the condition from one row per second (long) to one row per ID (wide).
  dataset <- dataset_long %>%
    select(ID, second, warmth) %>%
    mutate(second = str_c(variable_prefix, ".", second)) %>%
    pivot_wider(
      id_cols = ID,
      names_from = second,
      values_from = warmth
    )

  # Identify all second-by-second warmth variables created for this condition.
  warmth_vars <- names(dataset)[str_starts(names(dataset), paste0(variable_prefix, "."))]

  # Calculate each ID's average warmth across all available coded seconds.
  dataset[[average_name]] <- rowMeans(dataset[warmth_vars], na.rm = TRUE)

  # If all second-level warmth values are missing, rowMeans(..., na.rm = TRUE)
    # returns NaN because there are no numeric values left to average.
    # Convert NaN to NA so the video-level average is stored as missing.
  dataset[[average_name]][is.nan(dataset[[average_name]])] <- NA_real_

  dataset
}

section: Validate a finished wide warmth dataset
text:
Validate a finished wide warmth dataset
This function is the final data-quality stop point for the wide production datasets. It checks that there is one row per ID and that all nonmissing second-by-second warmth values are within 1–7 after code 0 has been converted to missing.


Show code
validate_warmth_dataset <- function(dataset, dataset_name) {

  # Stop if the finished dataset contains duplicate couple IDs.
  duplicate_ids <- dataset %>%
    count(ID) %>%
    filter(n > 1)

  if (nrow(duplicate_ids) > 0) {
    stop(
      dataset_name, " contains duplicate IDs: ",
      paste(duplicate_ids$ID, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  # Select second-by-second warmth variables while excluding ID and average variables.
  warmth_vars <- names(dataset)[
    names(dataset) != "ID" &
      !str_detect(names(dataset), "\\.avg$")
  ]

  # Stop if any nonmissing warmth value falls outside 1-7 after zero-to-missing conversion.
  invalid_values <- dataset %>%
    select(all_of(warmth_vars)) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols = everything(),
      names_to = "variable",
      values_to = "warmth"
    ) %>%
    filter(!is.na(warmth), warmth < 1 | warmth > 7)

  if (nrow(invalid_values) > 0) {
    stop(dataset_name, " contains warmth values outside the expected 1-7 range.")
  }

  message(dataset_name, ": data-quality checks passed.")
}

section: Process a set of reliability files
text:
Process a set of reliability files
This function sends each selected reliability CSV through the same process_single_warmth_file() function used for the original CARMA files. It then labels the condition, target person, and reliability coder.
Before returning the data, it checks that there is only one reliability source file for each ID × condition × person combination.


Show code
process_reliability_files <- function(files_full, condition) {

  # Stop if no reliability CSV files were found for this condition.
  if (length(files_full) == 0) {
    stop("No ", condition, " reliability files were found.")
  }

  # Build a file-level index before processing the second-by-second data.
  file_index <- tibble(
    source_path = files_full,
    ID = map_chr(files_full, extract_couple_id),
    person = map_chr(files_full, classify_reliability_person),
    condition = condition
  )

  # Stop if more than one reliability file exists for the same video/coder target.
  duplicate_files <- file_index %>%
    count(ID, condition, person) %>%
    filter(n > 1)

  if (nrow(duplicate_files) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Duplicate reliability source files found for: ",
      paste(
        str_c(duplicate_files$ID, duplicate_files$condition, duplicate_files$person, sep = " / "),
        collapse = "; "
      )
    )
  }

  # Process every reliability file with the same CARMA cleaning rules as production files.
  map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(file_index)), function(i) {

    processed <- process_single_warmth_file(file_index$source_path[i])

    processed %>%
      transmute(
        ID = ID,
        condition = file_index$condition[i],
        person = file_index$person[i],
        second = second,
        RC = warmth,
        source_file = source_file
      )
  })
}

title: Baseline Synchrony Calculation
text:
Synchrony Calculation


Show code
# Function to compute time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between dyad members
compute_blpwh_sync <- function(df, lag = 20, n_boot = 1000) {
  
  # Remove rows with missing data for both mom and partner variables
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(blmpwh), !is.na(blfpwh))
  
  # Check if there's enough data to compute lagged correlations
  if (nrow(df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 1: Pre-whitening via ARIMA to remove autocorrelation ---
  # Fit ARIMA models to each person's time series to account for their individual temporal patterns
  fit_mom <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blmpwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  fit_partner <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blfpwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  
  # If either model fails, return NA results
  if (is.null(fit_mom) || is.null(fit_partner)) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # Extract residuals (pre-whitened series) - these represent deviations from each person's own temporal pattern
  res_mom <- residuals(fit_mom)
  res_partner <- residuals(fit_partner)
  
  # Combine residuals and remove any remaining missing values
  residuals_df <- tibble(res_mom, res_partner) %>% drop_na()
  if (nrow(residuals_df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 2: Compute observed cross-correlation function (CCF) ---
  # CCF examines how mom's behavior at time t correlates with partner's behavior at time t+lag
  # Negative lags: mom leads partner; Positive lags: partner leads mom
  ccf_result <- ccf(residuals_df$res_mom, residuals_df$res_partner, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)
  observed_acf <- ccf_result$acf  # Cross-correlation values at each lag
  lags <- ccf_result$lag           # Lag values (e.g., -20 to +20)
  
  # --- STEP 3: Bootstrap to establish confidence intervals ---
  # Create matrix to store bootstrap results
  boot_corrs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(lags))
  n <- nrow(residuals_df)
  
  # Generate null distribution by randomly shuffling residuals (breaks temporal coupling)
  for (i in 1:n_boot) {
    x_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_mom, n, replace = TRUE)      # Resample mom's residuals
    y_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_partner, n, replace = TRUE)  # Resample partner's residuals
    boot_ccf <- ccf(x_boot, y_boot, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)   # Compute CCF on shuffled data
    boot_corrs[i, ] <- boot_ccf$acf  # Store correlation values
  }
  
  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap distribution
  lower_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  upper_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Determine significance: observed correlation falls outside 95% CI
  significant <- (observed_acf < lower_ci) | (observed_acf > upper_ci)
  
  # Return tibble with lag values, correlations, CIs, and significance
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(lags),
    acf = as.numeric(observed_acf),
    lower_ci = lower_ci,
    upper_ci = upper_ci,
    significant = significant
  )
}

title: Baseline Synchrony Calculation
text:
Synchrony Calculation


Show code
# Function to compute time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between dyad members
compute_blnwh_sync <- function(df, lag = 20, n_boot = 1000) {
  
  # Remove rows with missing data for both mom and partner variables
  df <- df %>% filter(!is.na(blmnwh), !is.na(blfnwh))
  
  # Check if there's enough data to compute lagged correlations
  if (nrow(df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 1: Pre-whitening via ARIMA to remove autocorrelation ---
  # Fit ARIMA models to each person's time series to account for their individual temporal patterns
  fit_mom <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blmnwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  fit_partner <- tryCatch(auto.arima(df$blfnwh), error = function(e) NULL)
  
  # If either model fails, return NA results
  if (is.null(fit_mom) || is.null(fit_partner)) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # Extract residuals (pre-whitened series) - these represent deviations from each person's own temporal pattern
  res_mom <- residuals(fit_mom)
  res_partner <- residuals(fit_partner)
  
  # Combine residuals and remove any remaining missing values
  residuals_df <- tibble(res_mom, res_partner) %>% drop_na()
  if (nrow(residuals_df) < lag + 1) return(tibble(lag = NA, acf = NA, lower_ci = NA, upper_ci = NA, significant = NA))
  
  # --- STEP 2: Compute observed cross-correlation function (CCF) ---
  # CCF examines how mom's behavior at time t correlates with partner's behavior at time t+lag
  # Negative lags: partner leads mom; Positive lags: mom leads partner
  ccf_result <- ccf(residuals_df$res_mom, residuals_df$res_partner, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)
  observed_acf <- ccf_result$acf  # Cross-correlation values at each lag
  lags <- ccf_result$lag           # Lag values (e.g., -20 to +20)
  
  # --- STEP 3: Bootstrap to establish confidence intervals ---
  # Create matrix to store bootstrap results
  boot_corrs <- matrix(NA, nrow = n_boot, ncol = length(lags))
  n <- nrow(residuals_df)
  
  # Generate null distribution by randomly shuffling residuals (breaks temporal coupling)
  for (i in 1:n_boot) {
    x_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_mom, n, replace = TRUE)      # Resample mom's residuals
    y_boot <- sample(residuals_df$res_partner, n, replace = TRUE)  # Resample partner's residuals
    boot_ccf <- ccf(x_boot, y_boot, lag.max = lag, plot = FALSE)   # Compute CCF on shuffled data
    boot_corrs[i, ] <- boot_ccf$acf  # Store correlation values
  }
  
  # Calculate 95% confidence intervals from bootstrap distribution
  lower_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  upper_ci <- apply(boot_corrs, 2, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # Determine significance: observed correlation falls outside 95% CI
  significant <- (observed_acf < lower_ci) | (observed_acf > upper_ci)
  
  # Return tibble with lag values, correlations, CIs, and significance
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(lags),
    acf = as.numeric(observed_acf),
    lower_ci = lower_ci,
    upper_ci = upper_ci,
    significant = significant
  )
}

blnwh_sync_summary <- blnwh_sync_results %>%
  mutate(significant = as.vector(significant)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(significant)) %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  summarise(
    # Basic counts
    n_significant_lags = sum(significant),
    has_any_significant = any(significant),
    
    # If significant, what's the strongest?
    strongest_lag = if(any(significant)) {
      lag[which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    strongest_acf = if(any(significant)) {
      acf[significant][which.max(abs(acf[significant]))]
    } else NA_real_,
    
    # Specific patterns
    has_concurrent = any(significant & lag == 0),
    has_mom_leads = any(significant & lag > 0),
    has_partner_leads = any(significant & lag < 0),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  )

pred_labels <- c(
  "female"       = "Sex (Male = 0)",
  "Zwave1age"    = "Age",
  "Zpeer_subuse" = "Peer Substance Use",
  "pub_timing"   = "Pubertal Timing")
  #"Zasp"         = "Autonomy Supportive Parenting"


tidy_params <- function(raw, cluster_cols) {
  raw %>%
    rename_with(~ "predictor_var", 1) %>%
    rename(omnibus_p = `p-value`) %>%
    pivot_longer(
      cols      = all_of(cluster_cols),
      names_to  = "cluster_raw",
      values_to = "log_odds"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      predictor_label = recode(predictor_var, !!!pred_labels),
      log_odds        = as.numeric(log_odds),
      cluster         = recode(cluster_raw,
                          "Cluster1" = "C1", "Cluster2" = "C2",
                          "Cluster3" = "C3", "Cluster4" = "C4"),
      cluster         = factor(cluster, levels = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4")),
      OR              = exp(log_odds)
    ) %>%
    select(predictor_label, predictor_var, cluster, log_odds, OR, omnibus_p)
}

c1_params <- tidy_params(c1_params_raw, c("Cluster1", "Cluster2", "Cluster3", "Cluster4"))
c3_params <- tidy_params(c3_params_raw, c("Cluster3", "Cluster4", "Cluster1", "Cluster2"))

apply_bh <- function(raw) {
  raw %>%
    rename(predictor = covariate, p_value = `p-value`) %>%
    filter(predictor != "Intercept") %>%
    mutate(
      p_value = as.numeric(p_value),
      p_adj   = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
      sig     = p_adj < .05

title: Predictor OR Line Graphs
text:
Build OR Data: Helper Function


Show code
# build_or_long():
#   params     = output of tidy_params() for a given reference class
#   pairs      = output of apply_bh() for a given reference class
#   ref_cluster = "C1" or "C3" — the reference cluster label
#   ref_num    = 1 or 3 — the numeric cluster number used in pairs columns
#
# Returns a long data frame with one row per predictor × cluster,
# with columns: predictor_var, predictor_label, cluster, log_odds, OR, or_color
# The reference cluster row is added with OR = 1.0 and or_color = color_reference.

build_or_long <- function(params, pairs, ref_cluster, ref_num) {

  pred_var_to_pairs_name <- c(
    "female"       = "bio_sexD",
    "Zwave1age"    = "Zwave1age",
    "Zpeer_subuse" = "Zpeer_subuse",
    "pub_timing"   = "pub_timing")
    #"Zasp"        = "Zasp")

  or_colored <- params %>%
    filter(cluster != ref_cluster) %>%
    rowwise() %>%
    mutate(
      pairs_pred = pred_var_to_pairs_name[predictor_var],
      is_sig = {
        hit <- pairs %>%
          filter(
            predictor == pairs_pred,
            (cluster_a == ref_num | cluster_b == ref_num),
            sig == TRUE
          ) %>%
          mutate(other = ifelse(cluster_a == ref_num, cluster_b, cluster_a)) %>%
          filter(other == as.integer(gsub("C", "", as.character(cluster))))
        nrow(hit) > 0
      },
      or_color  = case_when(
        !is_sig             ~ color_nonsig,
        is_sig & OR > 1     ~ color_sig_positive,
        is_sig & OR < 1     ~ color_sig_negative,
        TRUE                ~ color_nonsig
      ),
      sig_label = case_when(
        !is_sig             ~ "Not significant",
        is_sig & OR > 1     ~ "Higher odds (sig.)",
        is_sig & OR < 1     ~ "Lower odds (sig.)",
        TRUE                ~ "Not significant"
      )
    ) %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(predictor_var, predictor_label, cluster, log_odds, OR, or_color, sig_label)

  # Reference cluster row: OR = 1.0 by definition
  ref_rows <- params %>%
    filter(cluster == ref_cluster) %>%
    mutate(
      or_color  = color_reference,
      OR        = 1.0,
      log_odds  = 0,
      sig_label = "Reference (OR = 1.0)"
    ) %>%
    select(predictor_var, predictor_label, cluster, log_odds, OR, or_color, sig_label)

  bind_rows(or_colored, ref_rows) %>%
    mutate(
      cluster   = factor(cluster, levels = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4")),
      sig_label = factor(sig_label, levels = names(or_legend_colors))
    )
}

c1_or_long <- build_or_long(c1_params, c1_pairs, ref_cluster = "C1", ref_num = 1)
c3_or_long <- build_or_long(c3_params, c3_pairs, ref_cluster = "C3", ref_num = 3)

Figure: C1 as Reference — One Panel per Predictor (Line)


Show code
# Predictor display order and titles
pred_order  <- c("female", "Zwave1age", "Zpeer_subuse", "pub_timing")
pred_titles <- c(
  "female"       = "Sex (Male = 0)",
  "Zwave1age"    = "Age",
  "Zpeer_subuse" = "Peer Substance Use",
  "pub_timing"   = "Pubertal Timing")
  # "Zasp"        = "Autonomy Supportive Parenting")

# x-axis cluster label colors to match cluster colors
x_axis_colors_c1 <- cluster_colors[c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4")]

# Build and print one line graph per predictor (C1 reference)
plots_or_c1 <- lapply(pred_order, function(pred_var) {

  pred_data  <- c1_or_long %>% filter(predictor_var == pred_var)
  pred_title <- pred_titles[pred_var]

  pairs_pred_name <- c(
    "female"       = "bio_sexD",
    "Zwave1age"    = "Zwave1age",
    "Zpeer_subuse" = "Zpeer_subuse",
    "pub_timing"   = "pub_timing"
  )[pred_var]

  other_sig_c1 <- c1_pairs %>%
    filter(predictor == pairs_pred_name,
           cluster_a != 1, cluster_b != 1,
           sig == TRUE) %>%
    mutate(pair_label = paste0("C", cluster_a, " vs. C", cluster_b)) %>%
    pull(pair_label)

  fig_caption_c1 <- if (length(other_sig_c1) > 0) {
    paste0("Additional significant pairwise differences after BH correction (FDR < .05): ",
           paste(other_sig_c1, collapse = "; "), ".")
  } else {
    "No additional pairwise differences were significant after BH correction."
  }

  plot_obj <- ggplot(pred_data, aes(x = cluster, y = OR)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 1.0,
               linetype   = or_refline_type,
               color      = or_refline_color,
               linewidth  = 0.4) +
    geom_line(aes(group = 1),
              color     = "#BBBBBB",
              linewidth = or_line_size,
              linetype  = "solid") +
    geom_point(aes(fill = sig_label, color = sig_label),
               shape  = or_point_shape,
               size   = or_point_size,
               stroke = 0.5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = or_legend_colors, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_color_manual(values = or_legend_colors, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_y_log10(
      labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0.15, 0.15))
    ) +
    labs(title = pred_title, caption = fig_caption_c1) +
    theme_classic(base_size = axis_text_size, base_family = plot_font) +
    theme(
      legend.position    = "none",
      plot.title         = element_text(size = axis_title_size, face = "plain",
                                        hjust = 0.5, family = plot_font),
      axis.title.y       = element_blank(),
      axis.title.x       = element_blank(),
      axis.text.x        = element_text(size = axis_text_size, face = "plain",
                                        family = plot_font, angle = 0,
                                        hjust = .5, vjust = 1,
                                        color = x_axis_colors_c1),
      axis.text.y        = element_text(size = axis_text_size, family = plot_font,
                                        face = "plain"),
      axis.ticks.x       = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
      plot.background    = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA),
      panel.background   = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA)
    )

  print(plot_obj)
  cat("\n*Caption:*", fig_caption_c1, "\n\n")

  ggsave(file.path(fig_or_c1, paste0(pred_var, "_OR_C1ref_line.png")),
         plot   = plot_obj,
         width  = 14,
         height = 8,
         dpi    = fig_dpi,
         units  = "in",
         bg     = "transparent")

  plot_obj
})

    Covariate = factor(Covariate, levels = pred_order),

title: Odds Ratio Graphs
text:
Figure: Sex - C1 Reference


Show code
c1_sex <- c1_params %>% filter(predictor_var == "female")

ref_sig <- c1_pairs %>%
  filter(predictor == "bio_sexD",
         cluster_a == 1 | cluster_b == 1,
         sig == TRUE) %>%
  mutate(other = ifelse(cluster_a == 1, cluster_b, cluster_a)) %>%
  pull(other)                          # cluster numbers sig different from C1

other_sig <- c1_pairs %>%
  filter(predictor == "bio_sexD",
         cluster_a != 1, cluster_b != 1,
         sig == TRUE) %>%
  mutate(pair = paste0("C", cluster_a, " vs. C", cluster_b)) %>%
  pull(pair)                           # non-reference sig pairs for caption

c1_sex <- c1_sex %>%
  mutate(
    ast_label = ifelse(as.integer(cluster) %in% ref_sig, "*", ""),
    ast_y     = OR + max(OR) * ast_nudge_pct
  )

plot_title   <- "Sex (Female vs. Male)"
x_label      <- "Reference: C1"
y_label      <- "Odds Ratio - C1 as Reference"    
fig_caption  <- if (length(other_sig) > 0) { 
                  paste0("Additional significant pairwise differences after BH correction (FDR < .05): ",
                         paste(other_sig, collapse = "; "), ".")
              }  else {
                  "No additional pairwise differences were significant after BH correction."
 }
p_c1_sex <- ggplot(c1_sex, aes(x = cluster, y = OR, fill = cluster)) +
  geom_col(width = bar_width, alpha = bar_alpha,
            linewidth = bar_outline_lwd) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, color = ref_line_color,
             linewidth = ref_line_lwd, linetype = ref_line_type) +
  geom_text(aes(y = OR, label = round(OR, 2)),
            color = or_label_color, size = or_label_size, vjust = or_label_vjust) +
  geom_text(aes(y = ast_y, label = ast_label),
            size = ast_text_size, vjust = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cluster_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18)),
                     labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  labs(title = plot_title, x = x_label, y = y_label, caption = fig_caption) +
  or_theme + theme(plot.caption    = element_text(size = 14, hjust = .5, face = "plain", family = plot_font,
                                   margin = margin(t = 8)),
                    axis.title.x = element_blank() ,
                   axis.text.x = element_text(size = 32),
                   axis.title = element_text(size = 40),
                  axis.title.y = element_blank() )


ggsave(file.path(fig_or_c1, "bio_sexD_OR_C1ref.png"),
       plot = p_c1_sex, width = 14, height = 8, dpi = fig_dpi, units = "in")

title: Indicator Profiles
text:
Data Import
Indicator profile probabilities/means and paired-comparison significance tests across the latent class solution are read in from a local Excel results workbook from saved LatentGOLD results. Import code is included but not rendered below.


Wrangle Profile Data
Binary indicators (probabilities, 0–1) and continuous indicators (means, 0–3) are plotted together on a shared primary axis. Continuous values are divided by scale_factor before plotting so they fit the 0–1 primary axis; the right-hand secondary axis reverses that transformation to show the true 0–3 scale. scale_factor is defined in one place — adjust if indicator ranges change.


Show code
# Legend labels with cluster size in parentheses
cluster_sizes <- c("C1" = 35.6, "C2" = 33.7, "C3" = 15.8, "C4" = 14.9)

cluster_labels <- c(
  "C1"      = paste0("C1 (", cluster_sizes["C1"], "%)"),
  "C2"      = paste0("C2 (", cluster_sizes["C2"], "%)"),
  "C3"      = paste0("C3 (", cluster_sizes["C3"], "%)"),
  "C4"      = paste0("C4 (", cluster_sizes["C4"], "%)")
)

# Fill colors — no outlines
indicator_colors <- cluster_colors

# Scale factor: right axis max / left axis max (continuous max ~3, binary max 1)
# Continuous values are divided by this before plotting, then right axis
# multiplies back to show true scale. Edit here if any continuous value > 3.
scale_factor <- 3

# Continuous indicators — values can exceed 1 and read off the right axis
continuous_indicators <- c(
  "Problems from alcohol",
  "Sport Teams",
  "Extracurriculars",
  "Don't avoid problems"
)

# Negative panel: binary on left (0-1), continuous on right (0-3)
#   → continuous values divided by scale_factor to fit primary axis
# Positive panel: continuous on left (0-3), binary on right (0-1)
#   → binary values multiplied by scale_factor to fit primary axis
# This arrangement puts the 0-3 axes adjacent in the middle of the combined figure.

neg_continuous <- c("Problems from alcohol")
pos_continuous <- c("Sport Teams", "Extracurriculars", "Don't avoid problems")

profile_long <- profile_raw %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Cluster1, Cluster2, Cluster3, Cluster4),
    names_to  = "cluster_raw",
    values_to = "value"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    cluster    = recode(cluster_raw,
                   "Cluster1" = "C1", "Cluster2" = "C2",
                   "Cluster3" = "C3", "Cluster4" = "C4"),
    cluster    = factor(cluster, levels = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4")),
    Indicators = factor(Indicators, levels = unique(profile_raw$Indicators)),
    # Rescale for plotting:
    #   Negative: continuous / scale_factor (plots on 0-1 axis, reads off right 0-3)
    #   Positive: binary * scale_factor     (plots on 0-3 axis, reads off right 0-1)
    value_plot = case_when(
      Risk == "Negative" & Indicators %in% neg_continuous ~ value / scale_factor,
      Risk == "Positive" & !Indicators %in% pos_continuous ~ value * scale_factor,
      TRUE ~ value
    )
  )




BH Correction on Pairwise Comparisons
Non-estimable rows (p = “.”) and the Intercept block are dropped before correction is applied across all remaining tests simultaneously.


Show code
pairs <- pairs_raw %>%
  filter(Indicator != "Intercept", `p-value` != ".") %>%
  mutate(
    p_value   = as.numeric(`p-value`),
    cluster_a = as.integer(clustera),
    cluster_b = as.integer(clusterb),
    pair      = paste0("C", cluster_a, " vs. C", cluster_b),
    p_adj     = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
    sig       = p_adj < .05
  )




Profile Figure
Figure 1: Negative Indicators Left y-axis (0–1): binary indicators, read as probabilities. Right y-axis (0–3): continuous indicators, read as means.


Show code
fig_caption <- paste(
  "Note. Left y-axis (0\u20131) = binary indicators (probability of behavior).",
  "Right y-axis (0\u20133) = continuous indicators (within-class mean).",
  "Continuous bars are rescaled to the primary axis for display;"
)

# make_panel() takes explicit axis config so Negative and Positive can differ.
#
# Negative: left = binary 0-1, right = continuous 0-3
#   primary axis shows 0-1; sec.axis multiplies by scale_factor to show 0-3
#
# Positive: left = continuous 0-3, right = binary 0-1
#   primary axis shows 0-3; sec.axis divides by scale_factor to show 0-1

make_panel <- function(risk_label,
                       left_name = "" ,left_lim, left_breaks,
                       sec_transform, right_name = "", right_breaks) {

  df <- profile_long %>% filter(Risk == risk_label)

  ggplot(df, aes(x = Indicators, y = value_plot, fill = cluster)) +
     geom_vline(
  xintercept = seq(1.5, length(unique(df$Indicators)) - 0.5, by = 1),
  color      = "#DDDDDD",
  linewidth  = 0.4
) +
    geom_col(
      position = position_dodge(width = dodge_width),
      width    = bar_width
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = indicator_colors, labels = cluster_labels,
                      name = NULL) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      #name   = left_name,
      limits = left_lim,
      breaks = left_breaks,
      labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.03)),
      sec.axis = sec_axis(
        transform = sec_transform,
        name      = right_name,
        breaks    = right_breaks,
        labels    = number_format(accuracy = 0.1)
      )
    ) +
    labs(title = paste(risk_label, "Risk Indicators"), y = NULL, caption = fig_caption) +
    base_theme +
    theme(
      axis.text.x        = element_text(angle = 35, hjust = 1,
                                        size = axis_text_size),
      axis.title.y.right = element_text(size = axis_title_size,
                                        color = "gray40"),
      legend.position    = "none",
      plot.title         = element_text(size = title_size, face = "bold",
                                        hjust = 0.5),
          plot.margin       = margin(20, 0, 40, 100)
    )
}

# Negative: left=binary(0-1), right=continuous(0-3)
p_neg <- make_panel(
  risk_label    = "Negative",
  #left_name     = "Probability (binary indicators)",
  left_lim      = c(0, 1.08),
  left_breaks   = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2),
  sec_transform = ~ . * scale_factor,
 # right_name    = "Within-class mean (continuous indicators)",
  right_breaks  = seq(0, scale_factor, by = 1)
)

# Positive: left=continuous(0-3), right=binary(0-1)
p_pos <- make_panel(
  risk_label    = "Positive",
 # left_name     = "Within-class mean (continuous indicators)",
  left_lim      = c(0, scale_factor * 1.08),
  left_breaks   = seq(0, scale_factor, by = 1),
  sec_transform = ~ . / scale_factor,
 # right_name    = "Probability (binary indicators)",
  right_breaks  = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)
)

print(p_neg)


ggsave(
  filename = file.path(fig_indicator, "profile_figure_neg.png"),
     device = agg_png,
  plot     = p_neg,
  width    = 14, height = 6, dpi = fig_dpi, units = "in"
)

title: Portfolio Overview
text:
Projects


SPR Cup Analysis
A cumulative risk analysis using Add Health survey data, weighting structural disadvantage indicators by their empirical association with each substance-use outcome to build outcome-specific adversity composites, then testing protective factors against those composites.
Tools: SPSS (data cleaning), R


Baseline Warmth & Synchrony Processing
An end-to-end pipeline for CARMA-coded parent-infant warmth data, from raw second-by-second video coding through inter-rater reliability to time-lagged cross-correlation synchrony between mother and partner warmth during a baseline observed interaction.
Tools: R


Still Face Processing
A raw-to-analysis-ready pipeline for the Still Face paradigm, importing per-subject behavioral event logs, validating episode boundaries (Baseline / Still Face / Reunion), and computing duration and joint-attention variables for infant, parent, and dyadic behavior.
Tools: R, Python


Add Health: Risk-Taking Profiles & Predictors)
A latent class analysis of Add Health survey data, characterizing indicator and predictor profiles across classes, testing between-class differences via odds ratios and interaction effects, and validating class-predictor associations with the BCH three-step auxiliary variable method.
Tools: R

title: Portfolio Overview
text:
Background
Rachel Marcus, Ph.D., is a developmental psychologist whose work centers on adolescent risk-taking, parenting, prenatal substance exposure, and developmental cascades, with a broader interest in prevention science and early child development. She completed her doctoral training at Penn State in the Development, Risk, and Resilience Lab under Dr. Rina Eiden, building a methods toolkit that spans structural equation and latent variable modeling, latent class/profile analysis, and intensive longitudinal data analysis in R. She brings over seven years of experience across federally funded behavioral research, clinical trial management, and data infrastructure work.

title: Indicator Profiles — Standardized (Z-Score)
text:
Standardized Profile Panels
I also standardized based on the within class average for each indicator, allowing for a visualization of how each profile compares to the mean. The code used to create the figures is below.


Variable Labels


Show code
#Variable labels for plots
indicator_label_map <- c(
  WSDalc               = "Alcohol Problems",
  cigwhole             = "Cigarette",
  skipschool           = "Skipped school",
  liewhere             = "Lied about whereabouts",
  awayhome             = "Night out(unsanctioned)",
  dare_dum             = "Dangerous dare",
  seatbelt             = "No seatbelt",
  drvdrunk             = "Drove Drunk",
  BC_dum               = "Risky Sex",
  steal12M             = "Theft",
  phyfight             = "Fight",
  WSDsport             = "Sport Teams",
  WSDactivity          = "School Activities",
  avoidproblems        = "Problem Approach",
  disclose             = "Friend Disclosure",
  intitaterelationship = "Initiated Relationship")

# "Negative" = negative risk indicators; "Positive" = positive risk indicators
indicator_risk_panel <- c(
  WSDalc               = "Negative",
  cigwhole             = "Negative",
  skipschool           = "Negative",
  liewhere             = "Negative",
  awayhome             = "Negative",
  dare_dum             = "Negative",
  seatbelt             = "Negative",
  drvdrunk             = "Negative",
  BC_dum               = "Negative",
  steal12M             = "Negative",
  phyfight             = "Negative",
  WSDsport             = "Positive",
  WSDactivity          = "Positive",
  avoidproblems        = "Positive",
  disclose             = "Positive",
  intitaterelationship = "Positive")

# Desired x-axis order within each panel — edit to reorder bars
neg_order <- c(
  "WSDalc", "cigwhole", "skipschool", "liewhere", "awayhome",
  "dare_dum", "seatbelt", "drvdrunk", "BC_dum", "steal12M", "phyfight")

pos_order <- c(
  "WSDsport", "WSDactivity", "avoidproblems", "disclose", "intitaterelationship")




Standardization
Class probabilities and indicator values are read in from the dissertation’s saved SPSS output (a 4-class LCA solution with an auxiliary ASP scale). Each indicator is then z-scored so the plotted classes are on a common scale.


Show code
# Variable names present in the indicator map
indicator_vars <- names(indicator_label_map)

# Standardize each indicator across the full sample
sav_scaled <- sav_raw %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(indicator_vars), ~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))

# Compute within-class means of z-scores
# Class variable assumed to be named "class" — update if different in your file
zscore_long <- sav_scaled %>%
  select(`clu#`, all_of(indicator_vars)) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = all_of(indicator_vars),
    names_to  = "variable",
    values_to = "z_score"
  ) %>%
  group_by(`clu#`, variable) %>%
  summarise(mean_z = mean(z_score, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(
    cluster    = paste0("C", `clu#`),
    cluster    = factor(cluster, levels = c("C1", "C2", "C3", "C4")),
    label      = indicator_label_map[variable],
    Risk       = indicator_risk_panel[variable],
    label      = factor(label, levels = indicator_label_map[c(neg_order, pos_order)])
  )




Legend Labels


Show code
# Cluster sizes
cluster_sizes_z <- c("C1" = 35.6, "C2" = 33.7, "C3" = 15.8, "C4" = 14.9)

# Edit the description for each cluster here
cluster_descriptions <- c(
  "C1" = "High PR - Low NR",
  "C2" = "Low PR - Low NR",
  "C3" = "Low PR - High NR",
  "C4" = "High PR - High NR"
)

cluster_labels_z <- setNames(
  paste0(names(cluster_sizes_z), ": ", cluster_descriptions, " (", cluster_sizes_z, "%)"),
  names(cluster_sizes_z)
)
cluster_colors <- c(
  "C1" = "#44AA99",
  "C2" = "#88CCEE",   
  "C3" = "#882255",
  "C4" = "#DDCC77"   
)

# Colors — pulls from cluster_colors defined in _setup.R
zscore_colors <- cluster_colors




Z-Score Profile Panels
A horizontal reference line at z = 0 marks the sample average so it is immediately clear which profiles fall above vs. below the mean on each indicator.


Show code
# Function to create panel for profiles
make_zscore_panel <- function(risk_label) {

  # Set x-axis variable order
  panel_order <- if (risk_label == "Negative") {
    indicator_label_map[neg_order]
  } else {
    indicator_label_map[pos_order]
  }

  # Select columns from dataset
  panel_data <- zscore_long %>%
    filter(Risk == risk_label) %>%
    mutate(label = factor(label, levels = panel_order))
  
  # Recode for graph 
  panel_data <- zscore_long %>%
    filter(Risk == risk_label) %>%
    mutate(label = factor(label, levels = panel_order)) %>%
    mutate(mean_z = case_when(
      mean_z >  1.0 ~  1.1,
      mean_z < -0.5 ~ -0.6,
      TRUE          ~  mean_z
    ))

  # Create plot
  ggplot(panel_data, aes(x = label, y = mean_z, fill = cluster)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "solid") +
   geom_vline(
    xintercept = seq(1.5, length(panel_order) - 0.5, by = 1),
    color      = "gray63",
    linewidth  = .8
  ) +
    geom_col(
      position = position_dodge(width = dodge_width),
      width    = bar_width
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = zscore_colors,
      labels = cluster_labels_z,
      name   = NULL
    ) +
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(-.6, 1.1),
     # breaks = seq(-.5, 1.0, by = 0.5),
    #  labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.1),
    breaks = c(-0.5,  0, 0.5, 1.0),
  labels = c("Below -0.5", "0.0", "0.5", "Above 1.0"),
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))
    ) + 
    labs(
      title   = paste(risk_label, "Risk-Taking Indicators"),
      y       = "Mean (Standardized)",
      caption = "Mean standardized (z-scored) indicator values by latent class. Values below −0.5 or above 1.0 are capped for display."
    ) +
    base_theme +
    theme(
      axis.text.x     = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1,
                                     size = axis_text_size, family = plot_font),
      legend.position = "none", 
       plot.margin       = margin(40, 0, 40, 100)
    )
}

# Run function for each indicator set
p_zneg <- make_zscore_panel("Negative")
p_zpos <- make_zscore_panel("Positive")

# Save negative panel
ggsave(
  filename = file.path(fig_indicator, "zscore_profile_neg.png"),
  device   = agg_png,
  plot     = p_zneg,
  width    = 14, height = 8, dpi = fig_dpi, units = "in",
  bg       = "transparent")

# Save positive panel
ggsave(
  filename = file.path(fig_indicator, "zscore_profile_pos.png"),
  device   = agg_png,
  plot     = p_zpos,
  width    = 14, height = 8, dpi = fig_dpi, units = "in",
  bg       = "transparent")

title: Odds Ratio Graphs - Scales
text:
BH Correction on Pairwise Comparisons


Show code
apply_bh <- function(raw) {
  raw %>%
    rename(predictor = Covariate, p_value = `p-value`) %>%
    filter(predictor != "Intercept") %>%
    mutate(
      p_value = as.numeric(p_value),
      p_adj   = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
      sig     = p_adj < .05
    )
}

c1_pairsasp <- apply_bh(c1_pairs_asp)
c3_pairsasp <- apply_bh(c3_pairs_asp)

apply_b2h <- function(raw) {
  raw %>%
    rename(predictor = predictor_label, p_value = `omnibus_p`) %>%
    #filter(predictor != "Intercept") %>%
    mutate(
      p_value = as.numeric(p_value),
      p_adj   = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH"),
      sig     = p_adj < .05
    )
}
c1_pairsasp2 <- apply_b2h(c1_asp_or)
c3_pairsasp2 <- apply_b2h(c3_asp_or)

title: Resilience Analysis
text:
This analysis was originally developed for the 21st Annual Sloboda and Bukoski SPR Cup, presented at the Society for Prevention Research 34th Annual Meeting (Marcus et al. 2026). It tests a residual-based model of resilience using the Add Health dataset ((Harris 2013), specifically Waves I and III (N = 4,882) and can be broken down into the following steps:
Section 2: Wave I structural disadvantage indicators are used to build outcome-specific disadvantage composites(Marquez, Francis-Hew, and Humphrey 2023).
Section 3: Wave III outcomes are regressed on those composites (Miller-Lewis et al. 2013).
Section 4: The standardized residuals from those models become continuous resilience scores (better- or worse-than-expected adaptation given disadvantage exposure).
Section 5: Multilevel resilience factors (individual, family, school, community) are tested as predictors of resilience, first in the full sample.
Section 6: The sample is split into low- and high-disadvantage subsamples to distinguish between promotive effects (help regardless of disadvantage level) and protective effects (buffer specifically under high disadvantage).
Load Packages
All analyses use survey-weighted regression (survey) to account for Add Health’s complex sampling design, with gtsummary/flextable/gt for APA-style output tables.


code
library(gtsummary)   # regression summary tables
library(flextable)   # table formatting and export
library(gtools)      # quantile splitting 
library(haven)       # read SPSS .sav files
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling
library(survey)      # complex survey / weighted regression
library(broom)       # tidy model output
library(gt)          # formatted tables


The analytic dataset is the merged Add Health restricted-use survey data (AddHealth_AllData.sav), read in with haven::read_sav(). Import code is included but not rendered below.



Variable recoding, dummy coding, and composite construction for this project were done in SPSS prior to import into R, across four syntax files by domain (demographics, structural disadvantage, outcomes, protective factors). Each is excerpted below to document the approach.


Demographics.sps recodes core demographic variables (child sex, age, race/ethnicity) into analysis-ready measures, checking frequencies before and after each recode.
*****************************CHILD SEX.
*Q: What is your biological sex?
***check frequencies for zeros.
frequencies variables = bio_sex /statistics = all.
*male = 1, female = 2.

*create dummy code for child biological sex (female = 1).
if(bio_sex eq 1) bio_sexD = 0.
if(bio_sex eq 2) bio_sexD = 1.
variable labels bio_sexD
    "child biological sex".
value labels bio_sexD
    0 "male"
    1 "female".
execute.

*check frequencies of new variable.
frequencies variables = bio_sexD /statistics = all.



Disadvantage.sps (672 lines) builds individual- and household-level disadvantage indicators, including race/ethnicity dummy codes with missing-data recodes.

*****************************FAMILY SOCIOECONOMIC DISADVANTAGE COMPOSITE.
*Components: famincomecat (continuous $, higher = more income), pareduc_avg (0-8, higher = more education), parentemploy (0-1, higher = more employment).
**Standardizing each component to z-score then reverse code so higher is more disadvantage, then take the average of all variables.

*standardize based on weight filtered dataset.
delete variables  Zfamincomecat  Zpareduc_avg Zparentemploy.
    *delete variable if previously standardized with whole sample. 
temporary.
    *temporary can't be used with delete.
select if (GSWGT3_2 ge 0). 
descriptives variables = famincomecat pareduc_avg parentemploy /save.
*Creates Zfamincomecat, Zpareduc_avg, Zparentemploy.
execute.

compute Zfamincomecat_r = Zfamincomecat * -1.
variable labels Zfamincomecat_r
    "Family income z-scored reversed (higher = lower income = more disadvantage)".
execute.

compute Zpareduc_avg_r = Zpareduc_avg * -1.
variable labels Zpareduc_avg_r
    "Average parental education z-scored reversed (higher = less education = more disadvantage)".
execute.

compute Zparentemploy_r = Zparentemploy * -1.
variable labels Zparentemploy_r
    "Average parental employment z-scored reversed (higher = less employed = more disadvantage)".
execute.

compute famSES_disadv = mean(Zfamincomecat_r, Zpareduc_avg_r, Zparentemploy_r).
variable labels famSES_disadv
    "Family SES disadvantage composite: mean of z-scored reversed income, education, employment (higher = more disadvantage)".
execute.

frequencies variables = famSES_disadv /statistics = all.

reliability variables = famincomecat pareduc_avg parentemploy
    /scale('famSES') all /statistics = all.

*standardize based on weight filtered dataset.
temporary.
select if (GSWGT3_2 ge 0). 
descriptives variables = famSES_disadv /save.
*Creates Zfamincomecat, Zpareduc_avg, Zparentemploy.
execute.



Outcomes.sps (473 lines) constructs the substance-use outcome variable (alcohol, cigarette, and tobacco use composite), depression, general health, and educational attainment. Below is a exert from the final section of scoring the depression outcome.
*****************************CES-D DEPRESSION COMPOSITE (WAVE 3).
*9 items (all in same 0-3 direction after reverse coding H3SP7 and H3SP11 above).
*Sum score (0-27 range); Desch et al. (2023).

compute cesD_sum = sum(dep_bothered, dep_blues, dep_asgood, dep_concentrate, dep_depressed,
                       dep_tired, dep_enjoyed, dep_sad, dep_disliked).
variable labels cesD_sum
    "CES-D depression sum score Wave 3 (0-27, higher = more depressive symptoms)".
execute.

reliability variables = dep_bothered dep_blues dep_asgood dep_concentrate dep_depressed dep_tired dep_enjoyed dep_sad dep_disliked
    /scale('CESD') all /statistics = all.

frequencies variables = cesD_sum /statistics = all.

*standardize based on weight filtered dataset.
delete variables  ZcesD_sum.
    *delete variable if previously standardized with whole sample. 
temporary.
    *temporary can't be used with delete.
select if (GSWGT3_2 ge 0). 
descriptives variables = cesD_sum / save.



Protective.sps (887 lines) builds the protective-factor composites, several of which are reverse-scored so that higher values consistently indicate greater disadvantage.Below is an example of the data cleaning of one variable and then the creation of one protective factor composite.
***************************COMMUNITY RESOURCES - CONNECTEDNESS (ADOLESCENT REPORT).

*Note: Items reverse-scored here so higher = LOWER community resources (disadvantage direction),
*consistent with the structural disadvantage framing of this composite.
*Community Connectedness (Wickrama & Bryant 2003): 4 items, yes/no (0/1), summed 0-4.
*Reverse scoring: recode 1->0 and 0->1 so high score = LOW connectedness = more disadvantage.

if (H1NB1 eq 1) knowneighbR = 0.
    *knows neighbors = connected (reverse to 0=low disadvantage).
if (H1NB1 eq 2) knowneighbR = 1.
    *doesn't know = disconnected = higher disadvantage.
if (H1NB1 eq 6 or H1NB1 eq 8 or H1NB1 eq 9) knowneighbR = -99.
recode knowneighbR (-99 = sysmis).
variable labels knowneighbR
    "Does NOT know most neighbors (H1NB1 reversed, 1=low connectedness/more disadvantage)".
value labels knowneighbR 0 "knows most neighbors" 1 "does not know most neighbors".
execute.
    
***************************COMMUNITY CONNECTEDNESS INDEX (Wickrama & Bryant 2003).
*Items coded in protective direction (1 = connected):
*knowneighb, talkneighb, neighbwatch, nbhdsafe.
*Sum 0-4; higher = more connectedness = more protective.

compute commconnect = sum(knowneighb, talkneighb, neighbwatch, nbhdsafe).
variable labels commconnect
    "Community connectedness (Wickrama & Bryant 2003, sum 0-4, higher = more connectedness)".
execute.

reliability variables = knowneighb talkneighb neighbwatch nbhdsafe
    /scale('commconnect') all /statistics = all.
*alpha = .51.

frequencies variables = commconnect /statistics = all.


*standardize based on weight filtered dataset.
delete variables  Zcommconnect.
    *delete variable if previously standardized with whole sample. 
temporary.
    *temporary can't be used with delete.
select if (GSWGT3_2 ge 0). 
descriptives variables = commconnect / save.
*******************************************************************************
The cleaned file was exported and merged into AddHealth_AllData.sav for the R analysis above.




Add Health uses a complex, clustered, stratified sampling design. All regressions use the Wave 3 grand sample weight (GSWGT3_2_2) via the survey package to produce design-consistent estimates.
Missing Sample Weight at Wave 3
Respondents missing GSWGT3_2 were not part of the Wave 3 sample (e.g., lost to follow-up, deceased, ineligible) and should be excluded from analysis


code
#how many cases missing
cat("Missing GSWGT3_2:", sum(is.na(dat$GSWGT3_2)), "\n")


Missing GSWGT3_2: 1622 


code
cat("Non-missing GSWGT3_2:", sum(!is.na(dat$GSWGT3_2)), "\n")


Non-missing GSWGT3_2: 4882 


Filtered Dataset


code
# ── Subset to respondents with valid Wave 3 weight ────────────────────────────
dat_w3 <- dat |> filter(!is.na(GSWGT3_2)) #dat_w3 is name of filtered dataset 

cat("Analytic n after excluding missing weights:", nrow(dat_w3), "\n")


Analytic n after excluding missing weights: 4882 


Sample Weighted Dataset


code
# ── Specify survey design on the subsetted data ───────────────────────────────
# Use design_w3 as survey weight design in regressions
# svydesign() with ids = ~1 specifies no clustering beyond the given weights
# Add Health's Wave 3 grand sample weight (GSWGT3_2) adjusts for unequal selection probability and non-response so estimates generalize to the population

design_w3 <- svydesign(
  ids     = ~1,
  weights = ~GSWGT3_2,
  data    = dat_w3)

cat("Sum of weights:", round(sum(dat_w3$GSWGT3_2), 0), "\n")


Sum of weights: 22144327 





Create Table 1 to display the M, SD, and range of each analytic variable.


code
# ── Variable lists with display labels ────────────────────────────────────────
disadvantage_vars <- c(
  "minorityD"          = "Minority Status",
  "school_disadv"     = "School Disadvantage",
  "econhardship"      = "Economic Hardship",
  "famSES_disadv"      = "Family SES Disadvantage",
  "nbhd_subj_disadv"  = "Neighborhood Disadvantage (Subjective)",
  "cens_nbhd_disadv"  = "Neighborhood Disadvantage (Census)")

protective_vars <- c(
  "commconnect"       = "Community Connectedness",
  "commintegr_disadv" = "Community Integration",
  "opt_hopeful"       = "Optimism / Hopefulness",
  "selfesteem"        = "Self-Esteem",
  "self_efficacy"     = "Self-Efficacy",
  "parentchild_rel"   = "Parent-Child Relationship",
  "schoolconnect"     = "School Connectedness")

outcome_vars <- c(
  "cesD_sum"    = "Depression Symptoms",
  "subuse_W3"   = "Substance Use",
  "edattain_W3" = "Education Attainment",
  "genhealth_W3"= "General Health")

# ── Function: get weighted M and SD, and unweighted range ─────────────────────
get_desc <- function(var, design) {
  mn  <- as.numeric(svymean(as.formula(paste0("~", var)), design, na.rm = TRUE))
  vr  <- as.numeric(svyvar(as.formula(paste0("~", var)),  design, na.rm = TRUE))
  rng <- range(design$variables[[var]], na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    M     = formatC(mn,       digits = 2, format = "f"),
    SD    = formatC(sqrt(vr), digits = 2, format = "f"),
    Range = paste0(formatC(rng[1], digits = 2, format = "f"),
                   "–",
                   formatC(rng[2], digits = 2, format = "f")))
}

# ── Build rows for each variable group ────────────────────────────────────────
make_desc_rows <- function(var_named_vec, design, section_label) {
  rows <- lapply(names(var_named_vec), function(v) {
    d <- get_desc(v, design)
    data.frame(Variable = var_named_vec[[v]], M = d$M, SD = d$SD, Range = d$Range)
  })
  rows <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  rbind(data.frame(Variable = section_label, M = "", SD = "", Range = ""), rows)
}

desc_tbl <- rbind(
  make_desc_rows(disadvantage_vars,  design_w3, "Disadvantage Predictors"),
  make_desc_rows(protective_vars, design_w3, "Protective Factors"),
  make_desc_rows(outcome_vars,    design_w3, "Outcomes"))

# ── Build flextable ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
header_rows <- which(desc_tbl$M == "")

header_rows <- which(desc_tbl$M == "")

descriptives <- flextable(desc_tbl) |>
  set_header_labels(Variable = "Variable", M = "M", SD = "SD", Range = "Range") |>
  add_header_row(
    values    = c("", "Weighted Descriptive Statistics"),
    colwidths = c(1, 3)                                        # was c(1, 2)
  ) |>
  theme_apa() |>
  font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") |>
  fontsize(size = 11, part = "all") |>
  bold(part = "header") |>
  bold(i = header_rows, part = "body") |>
  width(j = 1, width = 3.0) |>
  width(j = 2:4, width = 1.0) |>                              # was 2:3
  align(j = 2:4, align = "center", part = "all") |>           # was 2:3
  padding(i = setdiff(seq_len(nrow(desc_tbl)), header_rows),
          j = 1, padding.left = 20, part = "body") |>
  add_footer_lines("Note. Means and standard deviations are weighted using the Wave 3 grand sample weight (GSWGT3_2). Range is unweighted.") |>
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "footer") |>
  italic(part = "footer")

The analytic sample reports moderate average levels of structural disadvantage (e.g., M = 0.52 school disadvantage on a 0–3 scale) alongside relatively high protective-factor scores (e.g., M = 4.15 parent-child relationship on a 1–5 scale), consistent with a normative, not exclusively high-risk, longitudinal sample.

Section 6: The sample is split into low- and high-disadvantage subsamples to distinguish between promotive effects (help regardless of disadvantage level) and protective effects (buffer specifically under high disadvantage).
Load Packages
All analyses use survey-weighted regression (survey) to account for Add Health’s complex sampling design, with gtsummary/flextable/gt for APA-style output tables.


code
library(gtsummary)   # regression summary tables
library(flextable)   # table formatting and export
library(gtools)      # quantile splitting 
library(haven)       # read SPSS .sav files
library(tidyverse)   # data wrangling
library(survey)      # complex survey / weighted regression
library(broom)       # tidy model output
library(gt)          # formatted tables


The analytic dataset is the merged Add Health restricted-use survey data (AddHealth_AllData.sav), read in with haven::read_sav(). Import code is included but not rendered below.

Add Health uses a complex, clustered, stratified sampling design. All regressions use the Wave 3 grand sample weight (GSWGT3_2_2) via the survey package to produce design-consistent estimates.

# ── Variable lists with display labels ────────────────────────────────────────
disadvantage_vars <- c(
  "minorityD"          = "Minority Status",
  "school_disadv"     = "School Disadvantage",
  "econhardship"      = "Economic Hardship",
  "famSES_disadv"      = "Family SES Disadvantage",
  "nbhd_subj_disadv"  = "Neighborhood Disadvantage (Subjective)",
  "cens_nbhd_disadv"  = "Neighborhood Disadvantage (Census)")

protective_vars <- c(
  "commconnect"       = "Community Connectedness",
  "commintegr_disadv" = "Community Integration",
  "opt_hopeful"       = "Optimism / Hopefulness",
  "selfesteem"        = "Self-Esteem",
  "self_efficacy"     = "Self-Efficacy",
  "parentchild_rel"   = "Parent-Child Relationship",
  "schoolconnect"     = "School Connectedness")

outcome_vars <- c(
  "cesD_sum"    = "Depression Symptoms",
  "subuse_W3"   = "Substance Use",
  "edattain_W3" = "Education Attainment",
  "genhealth_W3"= "General Health")

# ── Function: get weighted M and SD, and unweighted range ─────────────────────
get_desc <- function(var, design) {
  mn  <- as.numeric(svymean(as.formula(paste0("~", var)), design, na.rm = TRUE))
  vr  <- as.numeric(svyvar(as.formula(paste0("~", var)),  design, na.rm = TRUE))
  rng <- range(design$variables[[var]], na.rm = TRUE)
  data.frame(
    M     = formatC(mn,       digits = 2, format = "f"),
    SD    = formatC(sqrt(vr), digits = 2, format = "f"),
    Range = paste0(formatC(rng[1], digits = 2, format = "f"),
                   "–",
                   formatC(rng[2], digits = 2, format = "f")))
}

# ── Build rows for each variable group ────────────────────────────────────────
make_desc_rows <- function(var_named_vec, design, section_label) {
  rows <- lapply(names(var_named_vec), function(v) {
    d <- get_desc(v, design)
    data.frame(Variable = var_named_vec[[v]], M = d$M, SD = d$SD, Range = d$Range)
  })
  rows <- do.call(rbind, rows)
  rbind(data.frame(Variable = section_label, M = "", SD = "", Range = ""), rows)
}

desc_tbl <- rbind(
  make_desc_rows(disadvantage_vars,  design_w3, "Disadvantage Predictors"),
  make_desc_rows(protective_vars, design_w3, "Protective Factors"),
  make_desc_rows(outcome_vars,    design_w3, "Outcomes"))

# ── Build flextable ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
header_rows <- which(desc_tbl$M == "")

header_rows <- which(desc_tbl$M == "")

descriptives <- flextable(desc_tbl) |>
  set_header_labels(Variable = "Variable", M = "M", SD = "SD", Range = "Range") |>
  add_header_row(
    values    = c("", "Weighted Descriptive Statistics"),
    colwidths = c(1, 3)                                        # was c(1, 2)
  ) |>
  theme_apa() |>
  font(fontname = "Times New Roman", part = "all") |>
  fontsize(size = 11, part = "all") |>
  bold(part = "header") |>
  bold(i = header_rows, part = "body") |>
  width(j = 1, width = 3.0) |>
  width(j = 2:4, width = 1.0) |>                              # was 2:3
  align(j = 2:4, align = "center", part = "all") |>           # was 2:3
  padding(i = setdiff(seq_len(nrow(desc_tbl)), header_rows),
          j = 1, padding.left = 20, part = "body") |>
  add_footer_lines("Note. Means and standard deviations are weighted using the Wave 3 grand sample weight (GSWGT3_2). Range is unweighted.") |>

Family SES disadvantage is the strongest predictor across all four outcomes (|b| = 0.13–0.58), and minority status shows the largest effect specifically for substance use (b = -0.40) and education (b =-0.25). All predictor-outcome associations are significant at p <.001, supporting the use of each as a weighted component of its outcome-specific composite below.

title: SPR Cup Analysis
Resilience Analysis
text:
Structural Disadvantage Composites
Each outcome’s composite is a weighted average of the six structural disadvantage indicators, where the weight for each indicator is the beta extracted above (indicator value × its beta for this specific outcome). This means the same six indicators contribute differently to each of the four composites, based on each indicator’s empirical association with that outcome.






A predictor with a stronger relationship to depression, for example, is weighted more heavily in the depression composite than in the substance use composite. The descriptives of the structural disadvantage composites can be found in Table 3.



Compute Composites & Add to Dataset

title: Still Face Variable Dictionary
text:
The Still Face Paradigm (Tronick et al., n.d.) is a brief, structured interaction task used to study early social-emotional regulation and the caregiver-infant relationship. It has three phases, or episodes, which are described below:

Baseline (bl) - the mother engages in normal face-to-face play with her infant, establishing each dyad’s typical interactive style
a 15 second transition, where the mother looks away before returning her gaze towards her infant
Still Face (sf) - holding a neutral, unmoving expression for a set interval, while remaining present but unresponsive
Reunion (re) - the mother resumes normal interaction, and the dyad’s recovery is observed

Beacuse infants expect consistent, responsive interaction; the mother withdrawing it is a mild stressor that reveals how the infant regulates distress, and how the mother-infant dyad repairs afterward.
Observational coding, the data the below table is drawn from, captures this by having trained coders mark the onset and offset of discrete behavioral states (e.g. gaze direction, facial affect, vocalization, motor behavior) continuously throughout each episode. This results in raw data with timestamped start/stop events per behavior per subject, as seen in the sample raw data in (still-face-data-example?). This data must be imported, cleaned, and transformed into variables in the sample data dictionary table.
The code used to create the sample data is (still-face-data-example-code?) and the code to create the replicated data dictionary table is (variable-dictionary-code?).






Tip



Scientific relevance of Individual and dyadic differences: the magnitude of the still-face effect and the speed/completeness of reunion recovery are used as indicators of infant self-regulation, mother-infant synchrony, and attachment-relevant processes. Blunted still-face reactivity, minimal recovery, or atypical patterns (e.g., disorganized behavior, dysregulated affect) have been linked in the literature to risk factors such as maternal depression, prenatal substance exposure, and early adversity.
